overview.text: Beethoven’s Symphony No. 5 in C minor, Op. 67, is recognized especially for its opening motif. Beethoven noted early ideas in autumn 1803 and completed the full score in March 1808. The opening’s four-note idea—three repeated Gs followed by a lower E-flat—has a short-short-short-long rhythm, and Beethoven varies the motif through the work. It is sometimes called the “Fate” Symphony because biographer Anton Schindler attributed the phrase “fate knocks at the door” to Beethoven; Beethoven-Haus Bonn cautions that this account is doubtful. The Fifth and Sixth symphonies were first performed together at Beethoven’s Vienna concert in December 1808.

key_facts.text: Its full catalog title is Symphony No. 5 in C minor, Op. 67.
Beethoven began noting ideas in autumn 1803 and completed the score in March 1808.
The opening motif has three repeated Gs followed by a lower E-flat, with a short-short-short-long rhythm.
The Fifth and Sixth were first performed together in December 1808; at that concert, the Sixth was called No. 5, and their numbering was later switched.
The “Fate” nickname rests on a doubtful attribution to Beethoven, reported by biographer Anton Schindler.
